Mr. Formanullah Khan, Advocate instructed by Mr. Sharifuddin Chaklader, Advocate-on-Record ----- For the Appellant.
Mr. Khandker Mahbubuddin Ahmed, Senior Advocate, instructed by Mr. Md. Aftab Hossain, Advocate-on-Record ----- For the Respondent.
parties:
Abul Hossain ----- Defendant-Appellant
Vs.
Md. Islam ----- Plaintiff-Respondent
full_judgment:
2. Plaintiff-respondent filed a suit against defendant-appellant, being other Suit No. 31 of 1978 in the Court of 5th Munsif, Sadar, Chittagong for arrear rent, compensation and for eviction from the schedule shop premises situated at Chaktai Commercial Area, Chittagong. The plaint case, inter alia, is that one Kamaluddin inducted the defendant in the suit premises as a temporary monthly tenant at a rent of Tk. 65/- per month payable according to the Bengali Calendar in the following month; that the plaintiff purchased the suit premises from Kamaluddin by registered Kabala dated 26.11.76 and also from other co-sharers of the said suit premises by different Kabalas; that the said vendor Kamaluddin duly attorned the defendant to the plaintiff and the defendant upon acceptance of the plaintiff as landlord agreed to pay rent from the month, Magh, 1383 B.S. since the rent of Poush, 1353 B.S. was paid to Kamaluddin. The defendant, however, did not pay the rent or any rent as promised and the plaintiff had to determine the tenancy only serving a notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act on 18.2.78. 

 3. Defendant contested the suit by filing a written statement. His case is that the suit premises belonged to one Ahmed Sharif; that his son said Kamaluddin used to collect rent on his behalf till his death and thereafter Kamaluddin collected the rent on behalf of alleged heirs of Ahmed Sharif; that the shop was gutted in 1969 and the defendant constructed the structures at his own cost with permission of the original landlord Ahmed Sharif; that Kamaluddin received the rent upto Poush, 1383 B.S. but thereafter he refused to accept the rent. As such the defendant remitted the rent by postal money order on 26.2.74; that the money order was refused on 10.3.77. Thereafter defendant deposited the rent in House Rent Control Case No. 81 of 1977 on 19.3.77 and since then he has been depositing the rent regularly by impleading the plaintiff as a party in the House Rent Control case on 24.2.78; that the plaintiff does not require the suit and bonafide. His plea of construction and rebuilding are mere pleas; that notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act was not duly served, that the defendant does not admit the plaintiff as owner of the premises, nor plaintiff's vendor Kamaluddin did duly attorn the tenancy in favour of the plaintiff. It is emphatically denied that upon acceptance of the plaintiff as landlord he agreed to pay rent from the month of Magh, 1383 B.S.; the plaintiff not being owner of the suit premises is not entitled to bring the suit for arrear rent, compensation and ejectment against the defendant. Hence the suit is liable to be dismissed. 

 4. The trial court decreed the suit on the finding that notice under Section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act was duly served on the defendant; that the defendant is a defaulter as he was depositing rent in the name of Kamaluddin who was not the owner since Magh, 1383 B.S. and as such there was no valid deposit of rent rendering the defendant to be a defaulter and the plaintiff requires the suit premises for his bonafide purpose. 

 5. Appeal being filed by the defendant, the learned Subordinate Judge, however, found that after offering rent to kamaluddin for the month of Magh. 1383 B.S. which was returned, it is not denied that the defendant has been regularly depositing the rent of the suit premises. The notice dated 2.1.78 Ext. A shows that the plaintiff attorned the defendant with the fact that he purchased the suit premises from Kamaluddin. It is the case of the defendant that he received the notice on 17.1.78 and thereafter he impleaded the plaintiff in the House Rent Control Case. There is no iota of evidence that the defendant ever acknowledged the plaintiff prior to his sending the notice dated 2.1.78 Ext. A. The defendant is not a defaulter and the plaintiff does not require the suit premises for bonafide requirements. 

 7. Admittedly the defendant was a tenant at the rate of Tk. 65/- per month under Kamaluddin. It appears that the plaintiff, Md. Islam by purchase from the said Kamaluddin on 26.1.77 and from other co-sharers became the owner of the suit premises. Defendant paid rent to Kamaluddin upto Poush, 1383 B.S. and thereafter he sent the rent of Magh, 1383 B.S. by Money Order on 26.2.77 and the same being refused on 10.3.77. House Rent Case No. 81 of 1977 was filed by the defendant on 19.3.77. It appears from the materials on record that the plaintiff served notice Ext. A, dated 2.1.78 on the defendant to attorn him as landlord and the said notice was received by defendant on 17.1.78. Thereafter the defendant in the said House Rent Case No. 81 of 1977 impleaded the plaintiff along with the previous landlord by an amendment petition on 24.2.78 and started depositing rent in the name of Kamaluddin. The plaintiff served a notice under Section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act. Ext. 4 (A) on 18.2.78. Thus it appears that the defendant received the notice of attornment on 17.1.78 and thereafter without approaching the Plaintiff and without offering the rent to him deposited rent in the House Rent Control Case. The pertinent question in the facts of the present case is whether after receiving the notice of attainment from the plaintiff, could the defendant deposit the rent under Section 19(2) without offering the rent to the plaintiff. 

 8. The definite case of the defendant is that a doubt having arisen in his mind as to who is legally entitled to receive the rent he deposited the same in the House Rent Control Case by impleading the plaintiff along with the previous landlord. Section 19(2) of Premises Rent Control Ordinance reads as follows: 

 "Where any bonafide doubt or dispute has arisen as to the person who is entitled to receive any rent referred to in section 18 in respect of any premises, the tenant -(a) may deposit such rent, and (b) may continue to deposit every subsequent amount of rent which becomes due in respect of such premises until such doubt has been removed or such dispute has been settled by the decision of any competent Court or by settlement between the parties, within a fortnight of the date on which such rent becomes due or from the expiry of the time within which such rent is required to be paid under Sub-section (5) of Section 18." 

 Thus, it appears that in case of bona fide doubt or dispute as to who is entitled to receive any rent as per Section 18, the rent may be deposited within a fortnight of the date on which the rent becomes due or from the expiry of the time within which such rent is required to be paid under Sub-section (5) of Section 18. 

 9. Apart from serving notice, from the evidence of plaintiff himself it appears that the original landlord Kamaluddin introduced the plaintiff to the defendant and P.W.2 Binoy Kumar Biswas another tenant of Kamluddin and told them that the rent was to be paid to the plaintiff as the suit premises have been sold to the plaintiff and he was entitled to rent of Magh, 1383 B.S. P.W.2 Binoy Kumar Biswas another tenant of previous landlord Kamaluddin also corroborated the plaintiff in this regard and P.W.2 stated that since then he was paying rent to the plaintiff instead of paying rent to the original landlord Kamaluddin. The trial Court noticed the evidence of these two witnesses and held that there is no evidence on record to show that the defendant offered rent to the plaintiff after coming to know that the plaintiff purchased the suit shop or that the defendant tendered any rent to the plaintiff which he refused to accept. The question of bona fide doubt or dispute as to who is entitled to receive any rent pre supposes a dispute as to ownership of the premises. In the present case, the transfer was made under some registered documents by the undisputed owners of the premises. There is nothing on record to show that any one questioned the purchase of the suit premises by the plaintiff. Thus from the facts of the present case it is clear that there was nothing on record for invoking the provision of Sub-section (2) of Section 19 of the Premises Rent Control Ordinance. Hence, there is no bonafide doubt for dispute, but it was only a device on the part of the defendant to avoid payment of rent to the plaintiff. Further, the rent deposit case was started against the previous landlord when he allegedly refused to accept rent and there being nothing on record to show that the rent was offered to the plaintiff, the deposit of rent in the name of previous landlord by impleading the plaintiff would not save the defendant from ejectment. In the case of Basiruddin Ahmed and another Vs. Dhirendra Mohan Das reported in 1984 BLD(AD) 280, this Division held that the deposit in the House Rent Controller Case by impleading the transferee landlord will not save the tenant from ejectment. Consequently, the tenant is a defaulter in this case. Accordingly, learned Single Judge of the High Court Division rightly set aside the judgment of the lower appellate court and restored that of the trial Court.
